definitions.meaning: taps means strikes repeatedly, as with a mallet
plugs away means keeps working doggedly at something

explanation.definitionFit: To strike with a tool head is one sense; to keep pounding at a task persistently is the other.

clue.text: Hospital doctor without energy becomes a poet

indicators.note: without tells us to leave one piece out of the doctor's title

parts.note: a houseman is a junior hospital doctor in British usage
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A junior doctor, worn out, turns to writing verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' drops E from HOUSEMAN. A houseman is the British term for a junior doctor in a hospital; A. E. Housman wrote A Shropshire Lad.
explanation.definitionFit: A. E. Housman was an English writer of verse, author of A Shropshire Lad.

clue.text: H is here, in a very remote place

definitions.meaning: in the seven-letter word nowhere the central letter is H, so H sits at that word's centre
a very remote place is somewhere far from anywhere, in the back of beyond

explanation.surface: A letter's location is given as somewhere utterly remote.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading is literal: the fourth of the seven letters of 'nowhere' is H. 'in' is the link to the idiom for a far-flung spot.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a location so isolated that it seems to be nowhere at all; the first reading is a literal letter position.

parts.note: the glowing discharge seen on ships' masts in storms is named after this patron saint of sailors

explanation.definitionFit: St Elmo's fire is the electrical glow on masts, named after the patron saint of sailors, hence a saint linked with fire.

clue.text: Swimmer (but not related to the rays)

definitions.text: Swimmer (but not related to the rays)

parts.words: Swimmer (but not related to the rays)
parts.note: a fish whose name suggests sunshine, though the rays in the clue might suggest the flat fish family; it is named for the sun, not linked to its rays

explanation.definitionFit: The ocean sunfish is a large swimmer of the sea; its name invokes the sun, yet it has no connection with sunbeams or with skates.

indicators.note: in places the custom word inside the rearranged letters of the road
a road under repair is broken up and put back together, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: custom means habit or usage, here use

explanation.surface: A local tradition was stirred up by roadworks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'repair' rearranges ROAD to ARO D, and 'in' sets USE between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean stirred up or provoked into being, as feelings or action are.

clue.text: Mahler's third and Beethoven's fifth, in full versions, often dropped

definitions.text: Mahler's third and Beethoven's fifth, in full versions, often dropped

parts.words: Mahler's third and Beethoven's fifth, in full versions, often dropped
parts.note: the third letter of Mahler and fifth of Beethoven are the same letter, spelt out in full as a word, and Cockney speakers often drop it from words like house

explanation.surface: Concert programmes advertise complete symphonies that are frequently cut.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about symphonies, but Mahler's third and Beethoven's fifth are letters of the composers' names: both are H, and H written out in full is its spelt name, notoriously dropped in Cockney speech.
explanation.definitionFit: The spelt-out names of the letter H, which many English accents fail to pronounce at the start of words.

parts.note: O is a nought, zero, so no
a prohibition is a ban

explanation.surface: A seaside town in Scotland with no restrictions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' is a link. Oban is a ferry port and holiday town on the west coast of Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Oban is a coastal town in Argyll popular with holidaymakers and ferry travellers.

clue.text: No direct flight, up or down

definitions.text: No direct flight, up or down

parts.words: No direct flight, up or down
parts.note: a flight of steps that winds round rather than going straight, climbed or descended

explanation.definitionFit: A winding set of steps is a flight that never goes straight, whether ascending or descending.

definitions.meaning: a theatre helper who looks after an actor's costumes and helps them change
a kitchen sideboard with open shelves on which plates are displayed

explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the backstage costume helper; the other is the furniture item with shelves displaying crockery.

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters are made into something new, a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: A book title about Tom's adventures has been taken out of print.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like a noun about a book, but it is the anagram signal: the fifteen letters of TOM IN ADVENTURES are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone reserved and withdrawn does not show feelings openly.

clue.text: First of March, everyone in road to palace

indicators.note: First of picks the opening letter of the following word

parts.note: everyone means all

explanation.surface: On the first of March, everyone lines the avenue to the palace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link. The Mall is the ceremonial road in London leading to Buckingham Palace.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mall is the London avenue running up to Buckingham Palace.

definitions.meaning: easy means not heavy or demanding
day means daylight, the opposite of dark

explanation.definitionFit: Not difficult or burdensome is one sense; daylight, as in 'by day', is the other.

definitions.meaning: transfer means hand over, as a ball to a teammate
a ticket is a permit allowing entry or travel

explanation.definitionFit: To hand something on is one sense; a permit granting admission is the other.

definitions.meaning: smaller means lesser in size or importance
a key in music, as opposed to major

explanation.definitionFit: Lesser in importance is one sense; a musical tonality contrasted with major is the other.

definitions.meaning: stop means a punctuation mark marking a pause
a butterfly with ragged orange wings and a white mark on the underside

explanation.surface: Someone shouts to catch a fleeing insect.
explanation.definitionFit: A punctuation mark indicating a brief pause is one sense; a European butterfly with a white mark is the other.

clue.text: Stone Age artefact damaged in hotel

indicators.note: damaged means broken up, so the letters are reassembled differently

explanation.surface: A prehistoric relic has been broken while kept in a hotel.
explanation.definitionFit: A neolith is a stone tool or object from the later Stone Age.

indicators.note: ornamental suggests the spoons are fancifully worked, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A christening gift of decorative spoons from the godmother seems fitting.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who stands surety for a child at baptism is a sponsor in church usage.

parts.note: leagues means alliances or associations, unions

explanation.surface: Tennis serving errors are recorded in British competitions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foot-faults' is a tennis term, but here it means defects of the foot: painful swellings at the big-toe joint.
explanation.definitionFit: Bunions are painful deformities at the big toe joint, literally faults of the foot.

clue.text: Where passengers wait for a rough kiss on the head

indicators.note: on the places the kiss above the head in this down entry

parts.note: a buss is a hearty, rough kiss
head means top

explanation.surface: Someone waits for a careless peck on the head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' is a link; in a down clue 'on the' puts BUSS above TOP.
explanation.definitionFit: A roadside stop is the place where travellers queue for public transport.

definitions.meaning: someone who breaks things to pieces
dish is slang for an attractive person

explanation.definitionFit: Someone who breaks things is one sense; British slang for a stunningly attractive person is the other.

clue.text: Sign of leader of a jolly group?

parts.note: a jolly is slang for a Royal Marine, abbreviated RM
a group of musicians is a band

explanation.surface: The front man of a cheerful pop group wears a mark of rank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' is a link. 'jolly' looks like an adjective but is old naval slang for a Royal Marine, giving RM. A team captain wears one on the sleeve.
explanation.definitionFit: A captain wears a band on the sleeve to show leadership of the team.

clue.text: Ribston close to horse trading town

parts.note: Ribston Pippin is an old English variety of eating apple
by means near, close to

explanation.surface: A place near the horse market is named.
explanation.walkthrough: Appleby in Cumbria hosts a famous annual horse fair run by Gypsy and Traveller communities.
explanation.definitionFit: Appleby-in-Westmorland is known for its yearly fair where horses are bought and sold.

parts.note: dig is slang for understand, so the ones who understand are those who dig, and Aussies are nicknamed this

explanation.definitionFit: Australian soldiers and people are nicknamed with a word that also means people who dig, and dig is slang for understand.

parts.note: observed means saw

indicators.note: first of takes the opening letter of the Swiss word

explanation.surface: A Swiss traveller noticed garden gnomes for the first time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gnomes' here means short wise sayings, not garden figures.
explanation.definitionFit: Gnomes in this sense are pithy maxims, the same as old proverbs or adages.

clue.text: Marx's house full of air-raid precautions

definitions.note: read as Marx is, naming one of the comedy brothers

indicators.note: full of puts the precautions inside the house abbreviation

parts.note: ARP is the abbreviation for air-raid precautions, the Second World War civil defence service

explanation.surface: A Marx home is packed with wartime civil-defence gear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marx's' reads as 'Marx is'. ARP was Britain's Second World War civil defence organisation.
explanation.definitionFit: Harpo was one of the Marx Brothers, the silent one with the harp.

definitions.meaning: a military prison, especially on a ship

explanation.definitionFit: A naval or military lock-up is one sense; a two-masted sailing vessel is the other.

clue.text: Their leaves used as first-day covers?

definitions.text: Their leaves used as first-day covers?

parts.words: Their leaves used as first-day covers?
parts.note: in Genesis Adam and Eve covered themselves with leaves of this tree, the first covering; first-day covers are also stamp collectors' envelopes

explanation.definitionFit: Fig leaves were the first clothes worn by Adam and Eve, so the tree's leaves were the earliest coverings.

indicators.note: overthrown says the hidden letters are read backwards
the clue word that says the letters sit inside the next words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A despot ruled in the age of Cleopatra before being toppled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' marks the hidden run RAST in Cleopatra's time, and 'overthrown' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: A Russian emperor ruling with absolute power is a by-word for an autocrat.

parts.note: ground rents look like payments for land, but here are splits in the earth, measured for size

explanation.definitionFit: Earthquakes, which tear the ground, are measured for magnitude on this scale.

clue.text: Pair about to hire something to delight them

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the pair abbreviation wraps the hire word

parts.note: hire means lease

explanation.surface: A couple are about to rent something for their own enjoyment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks like 'about to', but it is the container signal; 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A crowd-pleasing act or thing is one that gives delight to those watching.

clue.text: Deliveries that get under the feet?

definitions.text: Deliveries that get under the feet?

parts.words: Deliveries that get under the feet?
parts.note: in cricket, balls bowled to pitch right at the batsman's toes, under the bat

explanation.definitionFit: In cricket these balls are bowled to land at the batsman's feet, beneath the bat; cricket is a bat-and-ball game popular in Britain.
